chapter.title: Input/Output Stream Format
chapter.para: The cg-conv tool converts between various stream formats.

section.title: Apertium Format
section.para: The cg-proc front-end processes the Apertium stream format, or can convert for use via cg-conv.

section.title: HFST/XFST Format
section.para: HFST/XFST input can be converted for use via cg-conv.

section.title: VISL CG Format
section.para:
The VISL CG stream format is a verticalized list of word forms with readings and optional plain text in between. For example, the sentence "They went to the zoo to look at the bear." would in VISL format look akin to:
"<They>" "they" <*> PRON PERS NOM PL3 SUBJ "<went>" "go" V PAST VFIN "<to>" "to" PREP "<the>" "the" DET CENTRAL ART SG/PL "<zoo>" "zoo" N NOM SG "<to>" "to" INFMARK> "<look>" "look" V INF "<at>" "at" PREP "<the>" "the" DET CENTRAL ART SG/PL "<bear>" "bear" N NOM SG "<.>"
Or in CG terms:
"<word form>" static_tags "base form" tags
Also known as:
"<surface form>" static_tags "lexeme" tags

In more formal rules:
If the line begins with "< followed by non-quotes and/or escaped quotes followed by >" (regex /^"<(.|\\")*>"/) then it opens a new cohort.
If the line begins with whitespace followed by " followed by non-quotes and/or escaped quotes followed by " (regex /^\s+"(.|\\")*"/) then it is parsed as a reading, but only if a cohort is open at the time. Thus, any such lines seen before the first cohort is treated as text.
Any line not matching the above is treated as text. Text is handled in two ways: If no cohort is open at the time, then it is output immediately. If a cohort is open, then it is appended to that cohort's buffer and output after the cohort. Note that text between readings will thus be moved to after the readings. Re-arranging cohorts will also re-arrange the text attached to them. Removed cohorts will still output their attached text.
This means that you can embed all kinda of extra information in the stream as long as you don't hit those exact patterns. For example, we use <s id="unique-1234"> </s> tags around sentences to keep track of them for corpus markup.

section.title: Niceline CG Format
section.para: Niceline input can be converted for use via cg-conv.

The Niceline format is primarily used in VISL and GrammarSoft chains to make the output more readable. Using the same example as for VISL CG format, that would look like:
They [they] <*> PRON PERS NOM PL3 SUBJ went [go] V PAST VFIN to [to] PREP the [the] DET CENTRAL ART SG/PL zoo [zoo] N NOM SG to [to] INFMARK> look [look] V INF at [at] PREP the [the] DET CENTRAL ART SG/PL bear [bear] N NOM SG .
Or in CG terms:
word form TAB [base form] tags TAB [base form] tags ...or quotes... word form TAB "base form" tags TAB "base form" tags ...or mixed... word form TAB "base form" tags TAB [base form] tags

In more formal rules:
If the line does not begin with < and contains a tab (\t, 0x09), then it is a cohort. Anything up to the first tab is the word form. Readings are tab delimited, where if the first tag is contained in [] or "" then it is taken as the base form. Tags are otherwise whitespace delimited.
Any line not matching the above is treated as text, same rules as for VISL CG format. Note that a tab character is required for it to be a cohort - a word or punctuation without the tab will be treated as text.

section.title: Plain Text Format
section.para: Plain text can be tokenized for use via cg-conv. It is a naive tokenizer that you should not use, and is only included as a last resort. Five minutes in any scripting language should give you a much better tokenizer.

The tokenization rules are simple:
Split tokens on any kind of whitespace.
Split punctuation from the start and end of tokens into tokens. Each punctuation character becomes a separate token.
Detect whether the token is ALLUPPER, Firstupper, or MiXeDCaSe and add a tag denoting it.
The token then becomes a cohort with one reading with a lower-case variant of the token as base form.

section.title: Binary Format
section.para: The binary format can be generated by cg-conv and can be parsed either by cg-conv or by the Python bindings. It is designed for faster parsing than the textual formats. The intended usecase is cases where the same input needs to be processed multiple times (such as when testing several grammars).

The stream begins with a header containing CGBF followed by a 4-byte version number (currently 1). After that, each packet begins with 1 byte indicating its contents. 1 is a window, 2> is a command, and 3> is text.
Command packets have a second byte identifying the command: 1 for FLUSH, 2 for EXIT, 3 for IGNORE, and 4 for RESUME. Commands which manipulate variables are represented in window packets.
Text packets consist of a 2-byte length followed by the contents in UTF-8.

Each window packet begins with 4 bytes specifying the length of the block and then the following structure:
window flags [2] > 1 = has multi-window dependencies tags [array of str] variables [array] mode > 1 = SETVAR (var = val) > 2 = SETVAR (var = *) > 3 = REMVAR var [tag] val or 0 [tag] text [str] text_post [str] cohorts [array] flags [2] > 1 = is target of a relation wordform [tag] static_tags [array of tag] dep_self [4] dep_parent or 0xFFFFFFFF [4] relations [array] tag [tag] head [4] text [str] wblank [str] readings [array] flags [2] > 1 = is subreading of predecessor > 2 = deleted baseform [tag] tags [array of tag]
Where arrays and strings are both encoded with a 2-byte length followed by the specified number of objects or UTF-8 bytes. Each item of type [tag] is a 2-byte index into the window-wide tags array.

section.title: JSONL Format
section.para: The JSONL format is for exchanging data with programs that already have a JSON parser. It is read with --in-jsonl and written with --out-jsonl in vislcg3, and with -j and -J in cg-conv. The cg-conv auto-detection picks JSONL if a line starts with { and no other format matched first.

The stream is UTF-8 with one JSON object per line. Each object is a cohort, a line of text, or a stream command, in stream order. The keys are the same as the VISL CG format stores, minus the markup:
Cohort: w wordform, without the "< >" quotes (string, required) wb word-bound blank (string) sts static tags (array of strings) rs readings (array of reading objects) drs deleted readings (array of reading objects) ds dependency self (number) dp dependency parent (number; 0 is the root) id cohort ID for relations (number) rels relations, as {"name": [ID, ...], ...} (object) z text after the cohort (string) Reading: l baseform, without the " " quotes (string) ts tags, including mapping tags (array of strings) s sub-reading (reading object) tr rules that hit the reading, only written with --trace (array of strings) Text: t one line of text, without the newline (string) Stream command: cmd the whole command, such as "<STREAMCMD:FLUSH>" (string)
Keys that are empty or don't apply are left out, and unknown keys are ignored.

Details:
A reading with several mapping tags in ts is split into one reading per mapping tag, as in the CG format. Sub-readings and deleted readings keep only their first mapping tag. The writer puts mapping tags last.
s nests: the sub-reading of a sub-reading is in its own s.
ds and dp are written whenever dependencies are in use (a dependency grammar, or -D in cg-conv). They are window-local numbers starting at 1, with 0 as the root, like #1->0 in the CG format. With --dep-absolute, or once a dependency spans windows, they are global cohort numbers, but the root is still 0. dp is left out when the cohort has no parent; dp equal to ds also means no parent. The reader always uses ds and dp; it doesn't need -D. Dependency tags such as #1->2 in ts are treated the same way as in the CG format.
When relations are in use, every cohort gets an id (its global number), so that any cohort can be a relation target. rels holds the cohort's relations as target IDs, and its presence (even as {}) marks the cohort as related, like the ID: and R: tags in the CG format. With --print-ids every cohort gets an id.
drs is written under the same conditions as ; lines in the CG format: with --trace and without --trace-no-removed. cg-conv always writes it. drs is read only with --deleted; otherwise it is ignored.
Text after a cohort is written as z, with its lines separated by \n and without the last newline. Other text is written as one t object per line. The reader attaches a t line to the preceding cohort, the same way the CG reader attaches text lines, so z and t are interchangeable after a cohort. An object with both w and t is a cohort, and t is ignored.
cmd accepts the same commands as the CG format; see Stream Commands. SETVAR and REMVAR can list several variables separated by commas. The writer outputs one command per variable. An unknown or malformed command is kept as text, with a warning.
Between IGNORE and RESUME, cohort lines are kept as text, the same way the CG reader passes them through.
Blank lines are skipped. Lines that are not valid JSON, not a JSON object, have none of w, t or cmd, or have an empty w are skipped with a warning. Values of the wrong type are ignored with a warning, and a reading without l gets the wordform as its baseform.
